The Federal Aviation Administration is days away from launching an artificial intelligence tool to help manage air traffic over Washington, D.C., and the airlines still cannot get answers to some basic questions about it, including whether they can opt out.

Politico reported Friday that despite roughly three months of near-weekly meetings, carriers remain unclear on whether air traffic controllers themselves will use the AI and whether airlines need to train staff on it. Industry officials described weeks of confusion over how deeply the system would be woven into daily operations, with one telling the outlet that people had been "freaking out" about it.

The panic eased, according to Politico, after agency officials told the industry the tool would be used in a limited way at first. Carriers had worried it might drive up cancellations and rescheduling in the name of relieving bottlenecks.

The system, called Strategic Management of Airspace Routing Trajectories, or SMART, will generate alternative routing options that travel through the FAA's existing channels to controllers. FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford has said a 90-day testing period will precede any wider rollout. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, who has faced scrutiny over the agency's handling of aviation safety, has promoted the effort.
